entries.title: Bears' handoff to G Joe Thuney on trick play disallowed
entries.summary: <p>The Bears were flagged for an illegal forward handoff on a trick play in the second quarter of Thursday night's game against the Patriots at Soldier Field.</p><p>The Bears put tight end Colston Loveland at left tackle and had left tackle Ozzy Trapilo line up to the right of their right tackle. Caleb Williams took the snap and handed the ball forward to left guard Joe Thuney, who ran for four yards.</p><p>Thuney, a former Patriots legend, was flagged because it’s illegal to hand the ball forward to an interior lineman.</p><p>The Bears were forced to kick a field goal after receiver Rome Odunze was flagged for offensive pass interference on the next play. </p><h3>Notes</h3><p>• Linebacker T.J. Edwards, who was listed as doubtful because of a hamstring injury Wednesday, was inactive.</p><p>• Cubs star Pete Crow-Amstrong and White Sox second baseman Chase Meidroth chatted on the field before the game.</p><p>• Patriots Pro Bowl cornerback Christian Gonzalez was downgraded to questionable with an illness before kickoff, but played.<br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Halftime: Bears lead Patriots 20-14 after wild ending to first half
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> are up 20-14 on the Patriots at halftime Thursday thanks mainly to some big plays by wide receiver Luther Burden and a timely interception by linebacker D'Marco Jackson.</p><p>They had a chance to go into halftime up 20-7 and getting the ball to begin the third quarter, but squandered that with a sloppy final play. With three seconds left, Patriots quarterback Drake Maye dumped the ball off to running back Rhamondre Stevenson, who ran to the end zone for a 48-yard touchdown.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="fr" dir="ltr">RHAMONDRE STEVENSON‼️<br><br>📺 Prime Video <a href="https://t.co/heXDiTFnzW">pic.twitter.com/heXDiTFnzW</a></p>— New England Patriots (@Patriots) <a href="https://x.com/Patriots/status/2113446816603570284?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 23, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Burden is at 130 yards and a touchdown on just four catches, and quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/01/money-isnt-everything-with-a-big-contract-in-reach-qb-caleb-williams-wants-to-make-sure-bears-keep-winning" >Caleb Williams</a> has completed 9 of 16 passes for 167 yards and a touchdown for a 113.3 passer rating.</p><p>Jackson ended the Patriots' best threat at scoring touchdown by picking off a pass from Drake Maye in the end zone. </p><p>The Bears jumped to a 10-0 lead by overwhelming the Patriots on both sides of the ball.</p><p>The Patriots’ opening drive ended on fourth-and-five at the Bears’ 45-yard line when nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon — Who else? — blitzed to sack Drake Maye. Gordon had three sacks Sunday against the Falcons in his season debut and leads all NFL defensive backs for the season.</p><p>Williams followed immediately with a 26-yard pass to Luther Burden to put the Bears in scoring position, and they eventually settled for a 43-yard field goal by Cairo Santos. He and Burden struck again on a 58-yard pass late in the first quarter to set up D’Andre Swift’s four-yard touchdown run.</p><p>The Bears had a chance to run away with the game when Williams hit Burden on a 24-yard screen pass for a touchdown and a 20-7 lead with 14 seconds left in the first half, but had an incomprehensible defensive lapse.</p><p>Maye hit A.J. Brown for 18 yards, then called timeout at the Bears’ 48-yard line with three seconds left. The Bears were in prevent defense with safeties Dillon Thieneman and Skyler Thomas at the goal line, and Maye threw underneath, seemingly harmlessly, to Stevenson.</p><p>The Bears had five players between Stevenson and the end zone at the time he caught the pass, plus defensive back Cam Lewis chasing him from behind, but he weaved through them all the way down the field for a touchdown.</p><p>The Bears get the ball to begin the second half.</p><p>Here are the Bears' inactives for the game:</p><p>QB Case Keenum*<br>RB Kyle Monangai (thumb, toe)<br>OL Jordan McFadden</p><p>DL Jayden Loving<br>LB T.J. Edwards (hamstring)<br>LB Jack Sanborn (concussion)<br>CB Nick McCloud</p><p>* - designated as emergency third quarterback</p>

entries.title: Bears pay tribute to Mike Ditka on 'Thursday Night Football'
entries.summary: <p>There’s been no plan made for a public memorial for Mike Ditka.</p><p>Thursday night, then, might have to suffice.</p><p>Playing their first home game since the man synonymous with their franchise died Oct. 9, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> paid tribute to the legendary coach and Pro Football Hall of Fame player at Soldier Field.</p><p>The Bears handed out fake mustaches to all fans and a headband in the style of Ditka's trademark sweater vest to the first 10,000. They held a moment of silence before playing the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/22/bears-patriots-mike-ditka-pay-tribute-head-coach-player-89-number" target="_blank" >Patriots</a>, the same team Ditka beat in Super Bowl XX.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/3a0znM7xEA0?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Bears hold moment of silence for Mike Ditka"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>"If it wasn't for Ditka, we wouldn't have the Super Bowl," former center Jay Hilgenberg said in an on-field interview aired on the scoreboard.</p><p>The Bears stenciled a football with Ditka's No. 89 on it onto the northwest sideline. They wore a matching patch over the hearts of their jerseys.</p><p>Chairman George McCaskey wore a navy Ditka jersey over his French blue dress shirt. Bears guard Jonah Jackson walked into the stadium wearing a white long-sleeved No. 89 jersey.</p><p>Ditka's number was the last one retired by the Bears.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/wDOhJ7_sET4?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Bears fans get Mike Ditka mustaches at Soldier Field"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Tom Borich and his 12-year-old grandson, Kieran Chucketts, both from Superior, Wis., came to pay their respects.</p><p>"I've been a Bears fan since the 1960s, but I was always by myself in the land of Packers and Vikings fans — until my son-in-law and grandson came into the picture,” Borich said. “Now I've finally got some Bears fans to root with me. It's been a wonderful time.</p><p>“Ditka embodies the toughness of Chicago and the toughness of the Bears. We're excited to be here."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr"><a href="https://x.com/jonahjackson73?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@jonahjackson73</a> reppin' Da Coach 🤝 <a href="https://t.co/7WjFZBbV1u">pic.twitter.com/7WjFZBbV1u</a></p>— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears/status/2113379171120386551?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 22, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Ditka’s Pro Football Hall of Fame display on the south concourse showed off a sweater vest and gold jacket. Ditka, who had 4,503 receiving yards from 1961-66, was the first tight end ever inducted into the Hall.</p><p>A private funeral for Ditka has already taken place.</p><p><i>Ashlee Rezin contributed.</i></p>

entries.title: CPS approves $300,000 for family of girl who endured years of racist bullying
entries.summary: <p>The mother of a Black student who endured racist bullying for more than two years at a predominantly white Northwest Side elementary school is set to receive a $300,000 settlement from Chicago Public Schools.</p><p>The city’s Board of Education unanimously voted to approve the payment at its monthly meeting Thursday, more than a year after the Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ published an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/06/13/black-girl-endured-racist-bullying-mostly-white-chicago-school-cps" target="_blank" ><u>investigation into the incessant bullying and failures</u></a> by the school administration to curb it.</p><p>The student’s mother, Sher’Ron Hinton, filed a lawsuit against the district in July 2025 accusing the staff at Wildwood IB World Magnet School of “willful and wanton conduct” and negligence for allowing her daughter to be subjected to “extreme acts of race-based bullying, sexual harassment and sexual abuse.”</p><p>Hundreds of pages of school incident reports filled out by Wildwood staff and emails from educators showed the girl, who the Sun-Times and WBEZ called Jada to protect her identity, was subjected to repeated racial slurs, body-shaming, encouragement to kill herself and, in one case, touching “in places I don’t want to be touched.”</p><p>She told school employees four times in fifth grade that she had suicidal thoughts.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f40000" entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson considers TE Cole Kmet's right knee injury serious
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> tight end Cole Kmet was carted off the field in the fourth quarter Thursday night after hurting his right knee.</p><p>Kmet caught a second-down pass from quarterback Caleb Williams and ran up the Bears' sideline, where he was tackled. Kmet went down immediately, was surrounded by teammates and coaches and was eventually taken to the locker room.</p><p>The tight end was cheered as he was carted into the northwest tunnel. He gave a thumbs up to fans.</p><p>The Bears ruled him out shortly, and coach Ben Johnson was grim about the outlook afterward.</p><p>“I don’t think it looked very good," he said.</p><p>For a coach who rarely reveals much about injuries, that’s his way of saying that was a serious one.</p><p>Kmet had three catches for 28 yards against the Patriots. The catch on which was injured was a big moment for the Bears, who held a six-point lead and were facing second-and-nine from their own 10-yard line. </p><p>Kmet, a second-round pick out of Notre Dame in 2020, is the Bears' most senior offensive player. He entered the game with seven catches for 59 yards on the season.<br></p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Bears K Cairo Santos 'annoyed' by miss even after booting career-long FG
entries.summary: <p>Cairo Santos wasn’t smiling in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ locker room even after hitting a career-long 58-yard field goal Thursday night to salt away the Bears’ 30-24 win against the Patriots.</p><p>He was still "annoyed" with himself after hitting the left upright on a 53-yard try earlier in the fourth quarter that would have put the Bears ahead by nine. Santos has missed a field goal in each of his last three games — a 43-yarder wide left against the Packers and a 56-yarder wide left against the Falcons.</p><p>“I’m having a hard time celebrating these moments,” he said. “I shouldn’t act this way. But I just feel lieke I’m hitting the ball way too good to have these misses happen. Even though they’re from 50-plus, I’ve been making them all the time.”</p><p>Santos said he hit the left upright because he was trying to play a draw.</p><p>Quarterback Caleb Williams had taken a sack on third-and-five from the Patriots’ 30 with 1:39 to play. New England defensive lineman Christian Barmore was hurt on the play. Johnson had wanted to punt, but talked to special teams coordinator Richard Hightower during the injury timeout.</p><p>He asked if Santos wanted to kick the 58-yarder. Santos had already told his position coach that he did. Kicking into the south end zone, Santos had made 60-yard kicks during warmups.</p><p>"Just thankful I got the opportunity to bounce back," he said.</p><p></p>

entries.title: Previewing Week 10's top high school football games
entries.summary: <h3><b>Class 8A</b></h3><p><b>Bloom at No. 22 York</b><br><b>6:30 p.m. Friday: </b>After sitting 3-3 at the end of September, York (6-3) now is one of the hottest teams in the state in the wake of consecutive victories against fellow West Suburban Silver powers Downers Grove North, Glenbard West and Lyons by a total of five points. A pair of two-way linemen — Purdue recruit Owen Roberts and Dayton commit Brayden Byford — has led the resurgence. Running back Chris Georgas and quarterback Zack Assaad pace a balanced offense. Bloom (3-6), in the second year of a rebuild under former Simeon coach Dante Culbreath, has a victory against playoff qualifier Champaign Centennial.</p><p><b>Warren at Naperville Central</b><br><b>7 p.m. Friday:</b> After leaning heavily on running back Aaron Stewart — now a freshman wrestler at Illinois — last season, Warren (4-5) is more balanced this fall. Junior Jonathan Randolph has rushed for 1,224 yards and 16 touchdowns, and senior Xavier Vinson has passed for 1,042 yards and 11 touchdowns with five interceptions. Naperville Central (5-4) has won four of its last five games, including 21-17 last week against Neuqua Valley. Simon Hayes threw for 197 yards and three touchdowns, including a pair to DuPage Valley offensive player of the year Mark Williams.</p><p><b>Stevenson at Lockport</b><br><b>7:15 p.m. Friday:</b> Stevenson (4-5) has won four of its last five games after an 0-4 start. Eli Sligal passed for three touchdowns, including a pair to Luke Clark, in a rout last week of Waukegan. Lockport (5-4) was one of the surprises of the postseason last year, reaching the Class 8A semifinals after a 5-4 regular season. The Porters also started slowly this season, losing their first three games. Their only loss since was to No. 1 Lincoln-Way East. Quarterback Griffin Russell has passed for 1,725 yards and 18 touchdowns. His favorite targets are Jaxson Little and Khairi Silas.</p><h3><b>Class 7A</b></h3><p><b>St. Laurence at Belleville East</b><br><b>3 p.m. Saturday:</b> A year after reaching the Class 6A semifinals, St. Laurence (3-6) has been hit hard by injuries and had 18 players sidelined at one point. Illinois-bound linebacker Sean Rice, the Vikings’ best player, just returned last week after hurting his ankle while running through a banner before a game. Belleville East (6-3), which lost its season opener 24-7 against Lincoln-Way West, has won four in a row. Quarterback Kingston Jones has thrown for 1,290 yards and seven touchdowns with five interceptions.</p><h3><b>Class 5A</b></h3><p><b>Mt. Vernon at No. 24 Providence</b><br><b>2 p.m. Saturday: </b>It has been a roller-coaster ride for Providence (6-3). Head coach Tyler Plantz abruptly was fired after the Celtics started 4-0 and were ranked No. 1 in Class 5A. (He’s now a volunteer assistant at Mount Carmel.) They’re 2-3 under interim coach Adam Nissen, including a victory against defending Class 6A champ Fenwick. Running backs Broden Mackert and Brayden McKay and quarterback Dominic Vita all have big-play capability. Mount Vernon (3-6) is on a four-game losing streak, during which it has been outscored 244-100.</p>

entries.title: After Bears' latest win, we can say it: Chicago sports seems to be having a moment
entries.summary: <p>Is Chicago having a sports moment?</p><p>Because with the reigning AFC champion Patriots on the lakefront Thursday for a prime-time game against the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> — with the Bears in the role of favorites — it sure felt so.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> just made the playoffs. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>’ Connor Bedard is back on the ice and skating with Patrick Kane. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" target="_blank" >Bulls</a> have rookie Caleb Wilson, who already is proving this town is big enough for two stars with that first name. Start with all that, amplify it with a Bears team that more than occasionally looks good enough to beat any opponent not from the NFC North, throw in Mike Ditka-inspired fake mustaches for as far as the eye can see and what do you have?</p><p>A moment, indeed.</p><p>Every major sports market has its heydays, Chicago included, though the truth is they’ve been few and far between. Boston, for one, has the Patriots coming off a Super Bowl appearance and the Red Sox, Celtics and Bruins all in winning windows, too. Do we have it that good here? Well, maybe we’re getting there.</p><p>The Bears, of course, are the key to the whole operation. If Caleb Williams is spraying the ball around to Luther Burden and Colston Loveland and the team is winning, every game day is a holiday. If the defense is giving up ridiculous Hail Marys and the team is losing, an entire city scowls into its soup. When the Bears are good, man, this place is on fire. But without them leading the way, it’s Sleepy City.</p><p>It was a bit funny to look back at the last time the Bears beat the Patriots at Soldier Field, in 2000. That’s so long ago that Tom Brady was a rookie riding the bench. That December day, the Bears had Shane Matthews at quarterback, James Allen carrying the ball 37 times, passes being caught by guys named Kaseem Sinceno, Scott Dragos and Macey Brooks. Those Bears, bound for a 5-11 finish, had to be one of the most who’s-who of ‘‘who?’’ Bears teams ever, so different from this one right down to the coaches — stoic Dick Jauron vs. incandescent Ben Johnson.</p><p>The Bears went 0-5 against the great Pats teams quarterbacked by Brady, giving up an average of 35 points and losing by an average of just more than 14. On one side, the most successful team in sports. On the other, rarely the cause of much excitement.</p><p>Win or lose, it felt so different this time, and that felt like something. It felt good.</p><p><b>TOMORROW’S HEADLINES</b></p><p><b>• Caleb Williams Takes Next Step:</b> Maybe some people were too quick to anoint him a superstar, but the quarterback’s play the last two games essentially has been coach Ben Johnson’s dream come true. Be very excited.</p><p><b>• The ‘Problem Child’ Is Exploding: </b>That’s how Williams refers to Luther Burden — as in, the second-year wide receiver is a problem for anybody trying to stop this offense — which is just perfect. What a weapon.</p><p><b>• What’s Wrong With Jaylon Johnson?</b> The cornerback is playing like the weak link of the defense. Can’t cover, can’t tackle, can’t seem to run well. Is he hurt? Is he unmotivated? Answers must come.<b>Williams Takes Next Step: </b>Maybe some people were too quick to anoint him a superstar, but the quarterback’s play the last two games has essentially been Ben Johnson’s dream come true. Be very excited.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/22/bears-grades-patriots-chicago-new-england-caleb-williams-drake-maye-ben-johnson-soldier-field" target="_blank" >Bears’ grades are in. entries.title: Bears' grades are in. How did they do against the Patriots?
entries.summary: <p>Say this for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/22/bears-inactives-vs-patriots-lb-t-j-edwards-out-with-hamstring-injury" target="_blank" >a 30-24 win against the Patriots</a> at Soldier Field: Giving Cairo Santos — far from the strongest-legged kicker in the sport — a shot at a 58-yarder to all but put the game away was utterly fearless. Crazy? That, too, but still fearless. It was an A-plus move by Johnson, who would've had a lot of explaining to do had Santos come up short. All's well that ends well.</p><p>Let's get to all the grades:</p><p><b>QUARTERBACK — A-</b></p><p>Caleb Williams became the first Bears quarterback to throw for 300 yards in consecutive games since the great Mitch Trubisky in 2018. He put it where wide receiver Luther Burden could run with it after the catch and fed tight end Colston Loveland as needed. You had to love it when the locked-in Williams gave Burden the business after a 58-yard gain for celebrating instead of getting back to the huddle, requiring a Bears timeout. You also had to be impressed when Williams stood tall, took a big hit and delivered a perfect ball to Loveland — who dropped it — then came right back on the next down with a 22-yard dart to Burden, despite being roughed on the play. A 21-yard completion to Rome Odunze on third-and-11 in the fourth quarter — again under a heavy rush — was Pro Bowl stuff. Williams did take a terrible sack in the final minutes, which potentially could have been very costly, but kicker Cairo Santos took him off the hook.</p><p><b>RUNNING GAME: B</b></p><p>The Bears just don’t have the same oomph without Kyle Monangai, but D’Andre Swift held things down admirably against a tough defense. A tip of the helmet to Swift for not missing any game time after a hard, straight-on hit to his left knee in the first quarter. It tore a big hole in his pants, baring a bloodied knee, but, hey, he’s a hockey player.</p><p><b>TIGHT ENDS: B</b></p><p>Loveland had a second consecutive big game and scored a touchdown, but his pair of drops left some bigger numbers out there. With an early catch, Cole Kmet became only the second Bears tight end to reach the 3,000-receiving-yard mark, joining Mike Ditka. Alas, Kmet appeared to injure his right knee late in the game and had to be carted off.</p><p><b>LINEBACKERS: B-</b></p><p>With T.J. Edwards inactive again, D’Marco Jackson made his presence felt with several hard hits and an interception in the end zone after running step-for-step with tight end Eli Raridon. Otherwise, the linebackers — especially Devin Bush — were flummoxed by the Patriots’ tight ends in coverage. Bush did make a huge third-down, open-field stop on quarterback Drake Maye that forced a punt in the fourth quarter.</p><p><b>DEFENSIVE BACKS: C</b></p><p>The Patriots’ 48-yard touchdown on the final play of the first half — a catch-and-run-run-run by running back Rhamondre Stevenson — involved some colossally bad defense by the guys in the back end. Jaylon Johnson’s effort at a tackle on the play was severely lacking. Yo, Dillon Thieneman? Act like a first-rounder and don’t let that happen.</p><p><b>SPECIAL TEAMS: A-</b></p><p>Santos gave fans the worst kind of 2018 flashbacks when he doinked a 53-yard field-goal attempt with eight minutes left and left the score at 27-21, giving the Patriots a chance to take the lead. But he more than made up for it on a three-field-goal night with a 58-yarder right down the middle to make it 30-21 and all but end the game. Who knew he had 58 in him? Tory Taylor had a 65-yard punt and Zavion Thomas a 47-yard kickoff return. Odunze also fell on the Patriots’ last-gasp onside kick.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="fr" dir="ltr">RHAMONDRE STEVENSON‼️<br><br>📺 Prime Video <a href="https://t.co/heXDiTFnzW">pic.twitter.com/heXDiTFnzW</a></p>— New England Patriots (@Patriots) <a href="https://x.com/Patriots/status/2113446816603570284?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 23, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/22/bears-inactives-vs-patriots-lb-t-j-edwards-out-with-hamstring-injury" >Bears hang on to beat Patriots 30-24 as Cairo Santos seals victory with career-long 58-yard field goal</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/22/bears-patriots-cole-kmet-carted-off-with-right-knee-injury" >Bears coach Ben Johnson considers TE Cole Kmet’s right knee injury serious</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/22/bears-handoff-to-g-joe-thuney-on-trick-play-disallowed" >Bears’ handoff to G Joe Thuney on trick play disallowed</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/22/bears-patriots-mike-ditka-pay-tribute-head-coach-player-89-number" >Bears pay tribute to Mike Ditka on ‘Thursday Night Football’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: After a year of unusual weather in Chicago, should you brace for winter?
entries.summary: <p>It’s been a year marked by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/06/chicago-deep-tunnel-historic-flooding-tarp-reservoir-weather-climate-change?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=070726%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=070726%20Morning%20Edition+CID_3748f51cc00a6f31c481d301486d2507&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=Deep%20Tunnel%20has%20never%20reached%20limit%20now%20is%20almost%20full%20after%20weekend%20of%20heavy%20rains&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" ><u>heavy rain</u></a>, a record number of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/08/27/200-tornadoes-illinois-2026" target="_blank" ><u>tornadoes</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/01/september-october-chicago-heat-wave-is-this-normal" target="_blank" ><u>heatwave</u></a>s. Then in mid-October, temperatures hit 88 degrees in Chicago. That beat the previous record for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/10/13/chicago-area-smashes-nearly-2-decade-record-high" target="_blank" ><u>hottest Oct. 12</u></a> set in 1988, according to the National Weather Service.</p><p>With all the unusual weather, what’s in store for winter?</p><p><b>Milder winter expected</b></p><p>Chicago can expect a milder winter due to a potentially “historically strong” El Niño, according to the National Weather Service’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/predictions/long_range/seasonal.php?lead=3" target="_blank" ><u>winter outlook</u></a> report released last week. </p><p>That means a 50% to 60% chance of above-normal temperatures this winter. But <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/10/15/a-historically-strong-el-nino-is-expected-to-make-for-a-milder-chicago-winter" target="_blank" ><u>the NWS said</u></a> even a mild winter will likely have “notable” stretches of cold weather and snowstorms.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.almanac.com/winter-extended-forecast-farmers-almanac" target="_blank" ><u>Old Farmer’s Almanac</u></a> also forecasts warmer weather with less snow for the Lower Lakes region, which includes Chicago. But winter will still be “difficult” with above normal precipitation. Early January and February will be the coldest periods this winter.</p><p>Meanwhile, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.farmersalmanac.com/extended-forecast" target="_blank" ><u>Farmer’s Almanac</u></a> forecasts near-normal temperatures for the Midwest, but winter won’t necessarily be mild. Chicago should expect “sudden cold snaps and brief snowy periods” interrupted by milder breaks, it predicted.</p><p><b>What is El Niño?</b></p><p>Something that seems more certain is a stronger El Niño.</p><p>El Niño is a weather pattern characterized by unusually warm temperatures in the Pacific Ocean. It leads to changes in the weather worldwide, including more rain across the southern U.S. and in Peru. That has caused destructive flooding, as well as drought in the West Pacific, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/ninonina.html" target="_blank" ><u>National Ocean Service</u></a>. (<a class="Link" href="https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/elnino/what-is-la-nina/" target="_blank" >La Niña</a> is characterized by unusually cold ocean temperatures in the Pacific).</p><p>El Niño typically occurs every two to seven years. The last was in 2023 into 2024, said the Sun-Times. The current one will almost certainly last through February 2027, the <a class="Link" href="https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/el-nino-set-become-very-strong-raising-risks-of-extreme-weather-2027" target="_blank" ><u>World Meteorological Organization</u></a> forecast in September.</p><p><b>What’s the impact of El Niño?</b></p><p>El Niño is already disrupting supply chains. Parts of Panama got much less rain this year, which has raised concerns about water levels that power the Panama Canal system.</p><p>As a result, the Panama Canal Authority began restricting traffic, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/10/08/magic-the-gathering-el-nino" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ reported</u></a>. This isn’t the first time El Niño has slowed down traffic at the Panama Canal; daily crossings dropped to 25 in November 2023.</p><p>More broadly, WMO expects El Niño to be potentially devastating around the world.</p><p>“El Niño in Spanish means boy child — but it has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world. We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies,” said <a class="Link" href="https://wmo.int/content/exceptional-el-nino-demands-exceptional-response" target="_blank" ><u>WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo</u></a>.</p><p>“This exceptional El Niño demands exceptional preparation and response. Never before in the 76-year history of the World Meteorological Organization have we launched such a major mobilization with National Meteorological and Hydrological Services who are on the frontline of delivering the forecasts and services to save lives and livelihoods,” she said.</p><p><b>How are these forecasts made? How accurate are they?</b></p><p>The NWS is a U.S. government agency under the <a class="Link" href="http://www.noaa.gov/" target="_blank" ><u>National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration</u></a> with nearly 150 weather <a class="Link" href="https://www.weather.gov/about/forecastsandservice" target="_blank" ><u>forecast offices and centers</u></a>. It collects and analyzes more than 6.3 billion observations per day. Forecasters use computers to <a class="Link" href="https://www.weather.gov/about/forecast-process" target="_blank" ><u>analyze observations </u></a>from surface stations, weather balloon readings, radar and satellite data. Then they use numerical, statistical and conceptual models to come up with forecasts. Forecasts that are further in the future are more uncertain.</p><p>A seven-day forecast is accurate about 80% of the time. But a forecast of 10 days or longer is accurate only about <a class="Link" href="https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/about/k-12-education/weather-forecasting/how-reliable-are-weather-forecasts#:~:text=A%20seven%2Dday%20forecast%20can%20accurately,90%20percent%20of%20the%20time." target="_blank" ><u>half the time</u></a>, the NOAA said.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.almanac.com/how-old-farmers-almanac-predicts-weather" target="_blank" ><u>Old Farmer’s Almanac</u></a> was first published in 1792 and is currently based in New Hampshire. It makes long-range predictions using meteorology, climatology and solar science — the study of sunspots and more techniques.</p><p>The Old Farmer’s Almanac predicts weather by “comparing solar patterns and historical weather conditions with current solar activity.” Results are often close to 80% accurate, it claims. But an independent study of five years of forecasts found that about 51% of its monthly temperature and precipitation predictions were correct, reported <a class="Link" href="https://www.cleveland.com/metro/2026/07/what-we-learned-about-how-accurate-the-old-farmers-almanac-forecasts-are.html" target="_blank" ><u>Cleveland.com</u></a><u>.</u></p><p>The Farmer’s Almanac was founded in 1818 and was traditionally published in Maine. Over the years, it has made <a class="Link" href="https://www.farmersalmanac.com/predicting-weather" target="_blank" ><u>weather predictions</u></a> using sunspot cycles, solar activity, tidal forces, the influence of the moon, winds over the equator and past weather patterns, according to its website.</p><p>Readers say its forecasts are 80% to 85% accurate, the Farmer’s Almanac claims. But other reports say its predictions are also accurate about <a class="Link" href="https://climavision.com/blog/weather-forecasting-and-the-farmers-almanac/" target="_blank" ><u>half the time</u></a>, according to Climavision, a weather technology and climate data company.</p><p>In 2025, the Farmer’s Almanac announced its closure, but new owners <a class="Link" href="https://www.farmersalmanac.com/farmers-almanac-saved-under-new-ownership-208-year-tradition-continues" target="_blank" ><u>saved</u></a> it from shutting down this year.</p><p><b>What’s the forecast for other parts of the U.S.?</b></p><p>Across the northern U.S., the NWS also expects warmer than normal temperatures from December to February. In addition, it forecasts wetter-than-average conditions across the southern U.S. and along the East Coast.</p><p>But there might be rough conditions ahead. “While higher chances of rain and snow may bring relief to drought-afflicted areas, too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides,” warned NWS director Ken Graham in its <a class="Link" href="https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/el-nino-looms-large-over-us-winter-outlook" target="_blank" ><u>winter forecast</u></a>. “Now is the time for communities and individuals to plan ahead for the upcoming winter.”</p>

entries.title: 3 years later, Kennedy Expressway traffic nightmare lives on
entries.summary: <p>If you’re among the legion of Kennedy Expressway commuters who had to put up with gridlock over the past few years during the massive roadwork project and swear you’ve never been in traffic this bad — you’re right.</p><p>An analysis of 22 years of drive-time data by WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times shows delays on the expressway between downtown and O’Hare Airport were the worst in more than two decades during the Kennedy Expressway rehabilitation project that began in March 2023 and ended last October.</p><p>Most of the longest Kennedy commutes on record occurred during the three-year project, as the state of Illinois spent more than $170 million working on the 7.5-mile stretch between downtown and the Edens Expressway junction.</p><p>And here's even more bad news for drivers: Despite Gov. JB Pritzker’s promise of "faster commutes" when he declared mission accomplished on the Kennedy project a year ago, the expressway has continued to post many historically bad travel times this year, WBEZ and the Sun-Times found.</p><p>That's as the separate Foster Avenue bridge reconstruction project over the Kennedy on the Northwest Side has lagged far behind schedule, with repeated delays, according to documents obtained by WBEZ and the Sun-Times.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8a0000" name="module-8a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>KENNEDY CONSTRUCTION: WHAT WE FOUND</b><br><ul id="rte-f3d36ee2-ce0e-11f1-aae6-ad083158f062"><li><b>WORST TRAFFIC IN 22 YEARS:</b> For most of the hours analyzed, the Kennedy Expressway “rehabilitation project” that was completed last year left drivers facing the worst travel times that have been seen on the expressway in 22 years, a WBEZ/Sun-Times analysis found.<br></li><li><b>12 EXTRA DAYS STUCK ON THE EXPRESSWAY:</b> A typical commuter traveling inbound in the mornings and outbound in the afternoons spent a total of <i>12 additional days</i> in traffic over the period since the roadwork began in March 2023 over what normally would have been expected.<br></li><li><b>JUNE 2025 WAS ESPECIALLY AWFUL:</b> The main roadwork wasn’t the only Kennedy headache. At times over the same period, the state of Illinois also had three other Kennedy-related projects going. Work on one of those — to replace the Foster Avenue bridge over the Kennedy — has faced repeated delays and still has no definitive end date.<br></li><li><b>THE WORST TRAFFIC CAME <i>AFTER</i> THE WORK WAS DONE:</b> The absolute worst time for outbound traffic was in June 2025— that was the only full month in which all four projects were going on at the same time. But the worst traffic and longest travel times on record for inbound traffic on the Kennedy in the afternoon and evening occurred earlier this year, in June, months after the rehab project ended last October.</li></ul></div> </div><p>The analysis of traffic data found that June 2025 saw the worst backups ever on the outbound Kennedy, with drivers facing an average commute time of 74 minutes to get from downtown to O’Hare between 2 and 3 p.m. on weekdays during that month. Average outbound travel times exceeded 65 minutes for each hour between noon and 7 p.m. on weekdays that month.</p><p>On the inbound Kennedy, headed downtown, the afternoon traffic jams have actually gotten worse since the end of the state project between the Edens junction and downtown.</p><p>There was no worse time in the afternoon to get from O’Hare to the Jane Byrne Interchange than between 5 and 6 p.m. on Mondays through Fridays this June — when the average drive time was an agonizing 75 minutes.</p><p>Some of the roughly 275,000 commuters who drive the Kennedy each day say the findings of the traffic-data analysis don't surprise them after facing years of crawling along the expressway and sometimes trying to navigate congested local streets in an often vain search for shortcuts.</p><p>“That was definitely the worst traffic I’ve ever had to deal with,” says Taylor Sticha, 35, who lives in Irving Park on the Northwest Side. “I have lived in Chicago my whole life. I take the Kennedy everywhere I go. And the last few years have been the worst by far.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" 20 minutes almost overnight.</p><p>So Sticha bought an e-bike to zip about 11 miles down the lakefront trail from the North Side to her job on the South Side. The commute on the e-bike is longer but faster than driving, taking her about an hour each way.</p><p>Sticha is among many commuters who went to extreme measures to deal with or try to avoid the agony of being stuck behind the wheel in barely moving traffic on the Kennedy.</p><p>Vivian Haritos, 46, who lives in Albany Park on the Northwest Side, echoes Sticha’s lament.</p><p>“I’ve commuted my whole life and traversed the same distance by car my whole life getting to and from school or work, and it’s just never been this bad,” Haritos says. “I’ve never experienced such horrific traffic.”</p><p>She says the construction “has negatively impacted my quality of life and even had me questioning my will to live at times.”</p><p>The impact of the Kennedy congestion on her psyche became a central and long-running theme of sessions with her therapist, said Haritos, a lifelong Chicagoan who works as a grant writer. By the time she got home after battling traffic, she says she'd be too tired to leave the house and battle traffic again to head out to see friends and family.</p><p>“I wasn’t mentally prepared for it,” she says. “It definitely affected my life negatively and affected relationships.”</p><p>Haritos says she loves Chicago, but she added, “It shouldn’t be this hard to get to and from work in the greatest city in the world.”</p><h3><b>Four road projects all at once</b></h3><p>The Kennedy opened to traffic as the Northwest Expressway 66 years ago, a few months before its eventual namesake, John F. Kennedy, took office as president. The Illinois Department of Transportation’s Kennedy Expressway rehab project began in March 2023, marking the first major work on the roadway in almost 30 years.</p><p>The project ended a year ago, marking a “major win for Chicago,” IDOT Secretary Gia Biagi said at the time.</p><p>The work involved construction on both the inbound and outbound lanes from downtown to the Edens junction, the Kennedy’s reversible express lanes, 24 exit and entrance ramps and dozens of “bridges that hadn’t been touched in decades,” Biagi said at an October 2025 event with Pritzker at which they marked the end of that work.</p><p>But, though it was the biggest, it was still only one of four significant roadwork projects on the Kennedy, at times overlapping. They cost taxpayers a total of about $225 million, records show.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-c30000" name="html-embed-module-c30000"></a><div style="min-height:613px" id="datawrapper-vis-5knSk"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/5knSk/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-5knSk"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/5knSk/full.png" alt="Overlapping road projects caused record traffic delays (Locator map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>In addition to the three-year Kennedy project, IDOT also recently finished making improvements to the Addison Street bridge over the Kennedy and to the span that carries traffic to and from the Kennedy on Ontario and Ohio streets over the North Branch of the Chicago River.</p><p>The fourth major project is the ongoing rebuilding of the Foster Avenue bridge. That work began in 2024 but has been plagued by setbacks, according to IDOT documents. Officials say the contractor has not told them when that work will be done.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The worst traffic on the outbound Kennedy was recorded in the summer of 2025 — the only period when work was happening on all four projects related to the expressway at the same time.</p><p>In a statement to WBEZ and the Sun-TImes, IDOT officials said all the work was necessary and overdue, but it “did not involve adding lanes or other capacity enhancements.” And they added, “We did anticipate a significant increase in delays as capacity was reduced by approximately 33%.”</p><p>Officials also warned that the public increasingly favored driving over public transit during the coronavirus pandemic: “Those behaviors continue to change but likely contribute to longer travel times for the time being.”</p><h3><b>Daylong rush ‘hours’</b></h3><p>WBEZ and the Sun-Times analyzed estimated travel times along the Kennedy dating to October 2004 and continuing through this August. The analysis covered 3.7 million estimated weekday travel times at five-minute intervals between 6 a.m. and 7:55 p.m.</p><p>That included inbound and outbound traffic times for the 17 miles between O’Hare and the Jane Byrne Interchange and statistics for how long it took to cover the expressway’s segments from downtown to Montrose Avenue — near the Edens junction – and from Montrose to the airport.</p><p>The analysis showed exactly how much the roadwork wreaked havoc with Kennedy commute times. Often, the kind of congestion you normally would expect only during rush hour was seen from early in the morning right on through evening.</p><p>In the nearly two decades prior to the start of the Kennedy rehab project, 4 p.m. was the peak hour for outbound traffic on weekday afternoons, averaging roughly 39 minutes. And 8 a.m. was historically the peak hour for inbound traffic on weekday mornings, averaging about 46 minutes.</p><p>Compare that to the traffic times on the Kennedy in June 2025, when outbound drivers faced an average drive of more than 50 minutes for every hour from 7 a.m. until 8 p.m. on weekdays. In effect, drivers faced a rush hour that lasted all day long.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-060000" name="html-embed-module-060000"></a><div style="max-width: 30rem;"><div style="min-height:1218px" id="datawrapper-vis-iApiU"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/iApiU/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-iApiU"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/iApiU/full.png" alt="Outbound weekday travel times (Scatter Plot)" /></noscript></div></div> </div> </div><p>Inbound traffic also experienced long stretches of rush-hour congestion. In June 2023, hourly traffic heading toward downtown on the Kennedy averaged more than 50 minutes from 7 a.m. until 11 a.m. and from noon until 7 p.m.</p><p>“This data is eye-opening,” says Joseph Schwieterman, a transportation professor who is the director of the Chaddick Institute for Metropolitan Development at DePaul University. “We see that motorists have lived through multiple years of congestion. And it’s not just rush hour. It’s all times of day.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-4c0000" name="html-embed-module-4c0000"></a><div style="max-width: 30rem;"><div style="min-height:1206px" id="datawrapper-vis-t4efN"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/t4efN/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-t4efN"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/t4efN/full.png" alt="Inbound weekday travel times (Scatter Plot)" /></noscript></div></div> </div> </div><p>Schwieterman says the Kennedy’s chronic traffic backups and the lack of a quicker rail link between O’Hare and downtown hurts Chicago drivers and also damages the city's reputation with visitors.</p><p>“You look at, by some measures, the country’s busiest airport at O’Hare, and a big, successful, global downtown, and you really have a tough time getting between the two,” Schwieterman says. “We have an expressway that’s, by national standards, among the most congested.”</p><h3><b>Worst traffic nationwide</b></h3><p>The Kennedy is the single biggest factor making Chicago’s freeway traffic the worst in the country — and among the worst in the world, one recent study found.</p><p>The typical driver in Chicago lost 112 hours to traffic in 2025, with a personal cost of $2,063 and a citywide loss of $7.5 billion, according to INRIX, a transportation analytics company based in Bellevue, Wash. Chicago ranked dead last in the country and second-worst in the world, with only drivers in Istanbul, Turkey, spending more time in traffic jams than Chicago’s motorists.</p><p>INRIX also identified the 10 most-congested sections of road in the United States in 2024, and five of them were in Chicago — including two segments of the inbound Kennedy and one portion of the outbound Kennedy.</p><h3><b>No end in sight on Foster Avenue bridge</b></h3><p>At the news conference last year, when the main Kennedy reconstruction project ended, the governor, Biagi and other state officials and labor leaders took turns heralding what they promised was a new and less-congested era for commuters.</p><p>“At a time of historic division in our politics, there is one idea we can all rally around, and that’s ‘traffic sucks,’” Pritzker said, laughing. But he added, “We’ll have faster commutes in the long run as a result of this.”</p><p>That’s not yet the case on the stretch of the Kennedy that slices through the Northwest Side toward O'Hare.</p><p>“It’s weird to pretend it’s done when it very clearly isn’t,” says Sebastian de la Torre, 25, a mechanical engineer who reverse-commutes each day between his job in Elk Grove Village and his apartment in the North Center neighborhood. “There’s hundreds of thousands of people that drive through there every day. Everyone sees that it’s not done.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-030000" Park, Tuesday, June 23, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The data analyzed by WBEZ and the Sun-Times backs him up. The inbound Kennedy actually got more congested after Pritzker’s news conference on Oct. 24, 2025. In June, the inbound Kennedy recorded its worst hourly averages in the 22-year period of the analysis for the 4 p.m. (72 minutes), 5 p.m. (75 minutes) and 6 p.m. (63 minutes) hours on weekdays.</p><p>And much of the most severe congestion for the portion of the Kennedy between O’Hare and Montrose has come this year. At some hours, in April, May and June this year, it would take you an average of more than 35 minutes just to get from the airport to Montrose — which still leaves you about eight miles from the Byrne Interchange.</p><p>The particularly bad traffic on the Northwest Side includes the area near the Foster Avenue bridge, which has been under construction for two years.</p><p>De la Torre moved to his apartment on the North Side in early 2025, after work began to tear down the bridge across Foster and build a new one.</p><p>“I never lived in a world where that bridge was up,” de la Torre says. “So I guess I’m excited to see what my commute is whenever they finish that bridge.”</p><p>De la Torre says he has tried to research when that day might finally come, but he’s been frustrated by a lack of answers from IDOT.</p><p>“It’s their job to be transparent to the public they serve allegedly,” he says. “I think it would help everyone to not be super-frustrated with the state of things in the state.”</p><p>IDOT initially rejected public records requests from WBEZ and the Sun-Times for meeting minutes and other documents pertaining to the four Kennedy-related roadwork projects, including the Foster Avenue bridge reconstruction, saying it would be too much work for them to gather and release those documents.</p><p>The news organizations, represented by attorneys Matt Topic and Josh Loevy, sued IDOT last year in Cook County court, citing violations of the state’s Freedom of Information Act. The agency relented recently and produced the disputed records and other documents related to the projects.</p><div class="ActionBox Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="ActionBox-content"> <div class="ActionBox-title">We want to hear from you</div> <div class="ActionBox-description">Tell us about your Kennedy construction horror story.</div> </div> <div class="ActionBox-cta"> <a class="Button" href="#kennedycontribly" target="_blank" >click here</a> </div> </div><p>Those records shed light on what’s really been happening with the Foster bridge project. They show it was plagued almost from the start by problems and delays.</p><p>The main contractor for the project, IHC Construction Companies of Elgin, submitted a “time-extension request” in July 2025, though state officials did not publicly announce those delays until this spring. Officials allowed the deadline to be pushed back from the end of May to Oct. 9 — but the work has continued.</p><p>In internal project correspondences, IHC executives said several problems have caused delays at the Foster site, but they said the biggest factor was slower-than-expected cooperation from the Chicago Transit Authority, whose Blue Line train tracks run down the center of the expressway at Foster.</p><p>Despite publicly pushing the completion date to the end of the year, officials still cannot say exactly when the project will be done, records show. The contractor has told officials that a second formal request will be filed for yet more time, citing weather-related issues and other delays, but has not yet provided officials with a new deadline.</p><p>“We have requested the revised baseline schedule from the contractor multiple times at the recent progress meeting, but we have not received it yet,” an engineer on the project wrote to state officials on Sept. 28, after IDOT told him a WBEZ reporter had filed a public records request for those documents.</p><p>Asked this week when the company’s work would be done, the project manager for IHC declined to comment, saying, “Since we are under contract with IDOT, these questions should go through them.”</p><p>IDOT officials now say they still expect the new Foster bridge to be open by the end of this year, although they added that electrical, sewer and landscaping work could continue there until the spring of 2027.</p><p>“This project is in a tight, urban environment and requires close coordination with the CTA and nearby railroad,” IDOT said. “We try our utmost to avoid them, but it’s not unusual for large, complex projects to have unforeseen issues develop throughout the course of the contract.”</p><p>Officials say they inform the public about delays “once there’s agreement on a revised timetable” with contractors.</p><p>State transportation officials also sought to brush aside concerns about the continued congestion near the Foster Avenue work site and beyond.</p><p>“Without looking at your data, we are confident based on our own observations and general feedback, that traffic overall on the expressway has improved since the project concluded as compared to when construction was taking place,” IDOT said in its statement to WBEZ and the Sun-Times.</p><p>“There could have been impacts from short-term disruptions over the summer, such as staging for the Foster Avenue project. We also have seen a busy festival season along with major events in the city temporarily inflate travel times over a short period of time compared to longer-term trends.”</p><p>But the long-running work at the bridge site has created gridlock not only on the Kennedy but also on streets in the quiet residential neighborhoods near the Foster construction. Drivers seeking to avoid the traffic have greatly increased the number of vehicles zooming down narrow side streets.</p><p>One homeowner in Jefferson Park even sent his City Council member’s office a door-camera video of a CTA bus taking a shortcut down a residential stretch of Mango Street.</p><p>“All the streets surrounding the Foster Bridge are also snarled, making it a terrible place to live and travel through right now,” one woman wrote to the office of Ald. James Gardiner (45th).</p><p>Records obtained by WBEZ show his office relayed concerns to IDOT, and a state official told a Gardiner aide in April that “unforeseen problems outside the control of the contractor” have led to additional delays.</p><p>The original budget to replace the Foster bridge was $25.2 million. But the estimated final cost now exceeds $28.6 million, records show.</p><h3><b>12 extra days per driver on the Kennedy</b></h3><p>Compared to how things were before the Kennedy rehabilitation began, average inbound travel times from O’Hare to downtown were nearly eight minutes longer at 8 a.m. on weekdays since the Kennedy work began.</p><p>Then, driving outbound at 5 p.m., you would have spent an average of more than 11½ minutes longer than before the roadwork began to get from downtown to the airport.</p><p>At that rate, someone who commutes to and from a job downtown from near the airport or beyond each day at those times has spent more than 17,000 additional minutes on the Kennedy between the start of the construction work in 2023 through August.</p><p>That works out to about 290 extra hours on the road — 12 full days stuck in worse-than-normal traffic.</p><p>Some commuters say they have struggled to cope with the situation.</p><p>Kristin Hoogenboom, who has to be at her job at a TV station downtown by 6 a.m., would wake up at 1:30 a.m. at her home in Elgin, get in a workout, drive to her husband’s office near downtown and take a nap there before starting her shift. That was better than waiting through construction delays, she says.</p><p>“That way, I didn’t have the stress of, ‘Oh, my gosh, am I gonna make it on time?’” says Hoogenboom, 53. “I did that for three years because I just didn’t want to deal with the IDOT Kennedy reconstruction project in the morning.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Kristin Hoogenboom who commutes around 3 PM each afternoon from downtown Chicago to Elgin, and deals with ongoing traffic on the Kennedy Expressway, poses for a portrait on Monday, October 12, 2026. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>She says taking a Metra train wasn't an option because walking alone across downtown in the predawn darkness was too dangerous. But she couldn't avoid the traffic on the way home, and it still takes her about 90 minutes to get to Elgin after work in the mid-afternoon.</p><p>“I changed my whole lifestyle because of IDOT for those three years,” Hoogenboom says.</p><p>Sticha, the woman who resorted to taking an e-bike to work, tried other ways to manage the construction-induced traffic before ultimately ditching her car for a new mode of transportation. She would bring a change of clothes and gym shoes and stop her commute home halfway to take a stroll on the 606 trail.</p><p>“Do a walk for 30, 40 minutes, get back in the car and then finish the commute,” she says. “Just try to cool myself down and get a little physical activity in.”</p><p>Public transit between her work and job were not convenient, and it was a bit far for her to bike each way. She turned to the e-bike and found a circuitous route that cut her commute each way to one hour.</p><p>To get to work in Pilsen, which is a 10-mile drive from home, she instead took a longer, 15-mile route on the e-bike, heading east to Lake Michigan, then down the bicycle path along the lakefront before cutting west over the 18th Street Pedestrian Bridge.</p><p>“If anything positive came out of this, it was getting that e-bike because now it’s one of my prized possessions,” Sticha said.</p><p><b>Using pain to stay awake at the wheel</b></p><p>The excessive traffic had an emergency-room nurse from the University of Chicago Medical Center worrying that she might fall asleep driving home to the North Side from her overnight shifts at the hospital in Hyde Park along the South Side’s lakefront.</p><p>“My normally 45-minute commute home turned into an hour-and-a-half commute home, and it was just too long for me to be able to withstand the powerful wave of sleep that would come over me,” Emma Squier says of her drive home in the early morning.</p><p>She tried blasting loud music.</p><p>“But that was just not effective,” she says. “So I would start doing these things to inflict pain on myself because that was really the only thing that would keep me awake. I would drive with one hand and bite the other hand while I was driving, or I would slap myself in the face.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8d0000" name="module-8d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>WHAT WE DID TO REPORT THIS STORY</b><br><br>To examine how the massive, three-year Kennedy Expressway “rehabilitation project” went, WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times:<br><ul id="rte-f3d36ee2-ce0e-11f1-aae6-ad083158f062"><li>Acquired nearly 10.5 million records of Kennedy Expressway travel time estimates — covering the period from October 2004 through August of this year — from Travel Midwest Stats, which provides real-time and historical drive-time statistics for area roadways primarily in Illinois and Wisconsin, including roads in Chicago and Milwaukee.</li><li>Analyzed estimated travel times at five-minute intervals from 6 a.m. to 7:55 p.m. for inbound and outbound Kennedy traffic between O’Hare Airport and the Jane Byrne Interchange.</li><li>Calculated travel times for inbound and outbound segments of the Kennedy between O’Hare Airport, Montrose Avenue and the Jane Byrne Interchange.</li><li>Filed public records requests with the state of Illinois for contracts, payments, meeting minutes, emails and other correspondence about four Kennedy-related road and bridge projects.</li><li>Sued the state when the Illinois Department of Transportation initially wouldn’t turn over the requested documents.</li><li>Interviewed Kennedy commuters who routinely drove the expressway since those projects started.</li></ul></div> </div><p>Squier says some coworkers from the night shift told her they would “roll their hair up in the window of the car, so their hair is constantly being pulled,” with the jolt of pain preventing them from dozing off.</p><p>In the ER at the UChicago hospital, Squier has seen what can happen to those who fall asleep while driving.</p><p>“Every day when I would get off work and get in my car to go home, I would be, like, OK, well, I really hope I don’t die, and I really hope I don’t kill somebody today,” she says.</p><h3><b>Labor pain on the Kennedy</b></h3><p>Another woman from the Northwest Side went into labor — and had to get from her home in Portage Park to Northwestern University's Prentice Women’s Hospital downtown — just as a major traffic jam was building on the Kennedy early on a weekday morning in September 2024.</p><p>“We start driving, and we get onto the highway at Irving Park Road, and we just immediately get stuck in traffic,” says Anna Behm, a librarian who’s now 41. “Just wall-to-wall cars, and we are kind of stuck on the highway.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Anna Behm, her husband Joey Falduto and their daughter Cricket Falduto pose for a portrait at Portage Park in Chicago on August 28, 2026. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Behm’s husband kept going on the Kennedy because no other route was better, according to the GPS. It ended up taking them more than two hours to get to Prentice, Behm says.</p><p>The data analyzed by WBEZ and the Sun-Times shows how much worse the traffic got even as Behm and her husband tried to get to the hospital. At 6:30 a.m. that day, the inbound trip from the airport to downtown was about 50 minutes. But that quickly ballooned to 97 minutes by 8:35 a.m..</p><p>Behm says she was suffering in the passenger seat, thinking, “This just feels inhumane to me. I feel like I’m being tortured right now. That’s how intense the pain was.”</p><p>She says she wasn't too mad at the state officials overseeing the construction project in the end because she made it to the hospital in time to give birth to a “beautiful, healthy baby girl.” She and her husband named the girl Cricket. They call her Kit.</p><p>Even so, it wasn't an experience Behm would ever want to go through again.</p><p>“It’s not like it took us two hours to get there because there was a blizzard,” she says. “It’s not like it was something that was an act of God.</p><p>“There really has to be a better way to move people around the city and do infrastructure work. That needs to happen without completely shutting down the main artery into Chicago.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-890000" name="module-890000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>METHODOLOGY</b><br><ul id="rte-f3d36ee2-ce0e-11f1-aae6-ad083158f062"><li>WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times acquired nearly 10.5 million records of Kennedy Expressway travel time estimates (throughout each day from Oct. 1, 2004 to Aug. 31, 2026) from Travel Midwest Stats, which provides real-time and historical drive-time statistics for area roadways primarily in Illinois and Wisconsin, including roads in Chicago and Milwaukee.<br></li><li>Nearly all of the travel times were provided at five-minute intervals for each hour throughout each day. The records included travel time estimates for various segments of the Kennedy Expressway: from O’Hare Airport to the Jane Byrne Interchange; from Montrose Avenue to the Jane Byrne Interchange; from the Jane Byrne Interchange to O’Hare Airport; and from the Jane Byrne Interchange to Montrose Avenue.<br></li><li>To measure weekday commuting times, WBEZ/Sun-Times focused its analysis on weekday travel time estimates for a 14-hour block, starting at 6 a.m. and ending at 7:55 p.m. For historical comparisons, WBEZ/Sun-Times calculated hourly travel time averages over the course of each month from October 2004 through August 2026.<br></li><li>WBEZ/Sun-Times calculated travel time estimates from Montrose to O’Hare by taking the difference between travel time estimates for the Byrne Interchange-to-O’Hare and Byrne Interchange-to-Montrose segments starting at the same time. Estimated hourly travel time averages for O’Hare to Montrose were calculated by taking the difference between the hourly travel time averages for the O’Hare-to-Byrne Interchange and Montrose-to-Byrne Interchange segments ending during the same hour.</li></ul></div> </div><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="kennedycontribly" name="kennedycontribly"></a><div class="contribly-contribute-v2" data-client="b20193c8-5c0c-4a5b-a770-64305c544c4e" data-assignment="8c5de317-7b05-4cf0-b372-b369c03e93d7" data-display="inline" data-language="en-gb"></div><script type="text/javascript" src="https://s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/contribly-widgets/contribute/contribute-v2.5.js"></script> </div> </div><p><i>Dan Mihalopoulos is an investigative reporter for WBEZ. Alden Loury is data projects editor.</i></p><p><i>Contributing: Justin Myers</i></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Grandparents worry about drug use around grandchild
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Our 24-year-old daughter, "Becca," and her 26-year-old boyfriend, "Jason," (the father of our 7-year-old granddaughter) recently bought a home. Jason works only part time — if he works at all — and has no interest in a full-time job.</p><p>One issue, however, really weighs heavily on our minds. Whenever we pick up our granddaughter (which we do quite often) we are almost knocked over by the smell of marijuana in their home. My husband and I have voiced our concerns about this more than once, to no avail. Our other children have mentioned the strong odor in her home as well.</p><p>My husband and I can't stand the thought of our granddaughter living in that environment, but we don't know what we should do about it. Abby, what do you advise? — <i>WORRIED ABOUT THE WEED IN INDIANA</i></p><p><b>DEAR WORRIED:</b> You and your husband should continue having a serious conversation with your daughter about this. Tell her you smell a strong marijuana odor when you pick your granddaughter up, and that you are worried about her inhaling the smoke, because it's unhealthy for children. Perhaps she and her boyfriend can choose to smoke outside their house when they feel the need to get high.</p><p>Inform them that if the child ever inhales enough secondhand smoke to test positive for THC, there could be serious legal repercussions (beyond the fact that — as you probably know — cannabis use is still illegal in Indiana).</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband, who is 86, has an indirect communication style. He'll say something like, "I need to do some pruning on the climbing rose, but it's too high for me to reach." I ask specific questions to determine what exactly, if anything, he wants me to do, but his responses are often vague. An example: I will ask, "Are you asking me to set up the ladder for you?" to which he might reply, "I can't reach the top of the roses."</p><p>No matter how many questions I ask, he resists giving me a direct answer. This frustrates me, and it frustrates him that I don't get his meaning instantly. Is there anything I can do to cut to the chase so I'll know what he's asking me to do? I'm happy to help him; I just want to know what he wants without the interrogation. — <i>VERBAL DANCE PARTNER</i></p><p><b>DEAR PARTNER:</b> What you have described is normal in households or regions (including East and Southeast Asia and parts of Europe) where people are taught to prioritize the comfort of others. In those cultures, it's considered rude and aggressive to make a direct request, even of a loved one.</p><p>Because he may have learned these values from his parents, know that this may be a lifelong habit that would be hard for him to break. If you ask him directly to change his ways, he may regard that as overbearing. Fortunately, you seem to have mostly cracked the code. You know his offhand remarks are actually requests, so do your best to help in ways that make sense to you. If you sometimes don't deliver exactly what he's looking for, it's up to him to clarify.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Poignant words touch reader who had recent cancer scare
entries.summary: <p>Kudos to Neil Steinberg on his happy and heartwarming <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/10/15/open-letter-pope-leo-xiv-lung-cancer-steinberg" >column</a> written as a letter to Pope Leo XIV. I would also like to offer my prayers and well wishes to Neil's sister, Debbie. She sounds like an amazing individual, and I hope she continues to fight her illness with the bravery and determination that she’s exhibited.</p><p>I recently went in to have a spot removed from my kidney. During the operation, my surgeon discovered the growth to be an aggressive Stage 3 clear cell cancer, and the entire left kidney needed to be removed. Though I had been alerted by my surgeon that this could happen, the aftermath was a bit jarring. My family and my doctors from Advocate Lutheran General Hospital have been so supportive and upbeat, that my recovery has gone very well.</p><p>I agree with proverb “a cheerful heart is good medicine.” I would also add that “a cheerful heart is good medicine" for healthy people too. I have tried living my life with a positive attitude and a sense of humor. I’ve always believed that stress kills, so being happy works well for me. I truly believe I’m a very fortunate man. My latest health ordeal was a slight setback for this recent retiree; but there are far more many people who are suffering and struggling more than me. </p><p><i>Rick Kalin, Belmont Heights</i></p><h3>An act of treachery</h3><h3></h3><p>It's now clearly in the open. There's no doubt President Donald Trump is actively aiding and abetting Russia — no ally of the United States — by <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/18/wright-defends-trump-russia-diesel-deal-01125781" target="_blank" >purchasing</a> Russian diesel fuel, delaying or denying Ukraine <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/10/18/nx-s1-6007382/ukraine-us-starshield-starlink-what-to-know-trump" target="_blank" >Starshield and Starlink</a> intelligence, <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-decision-to-waive-russian-sanctions-outrages-congress-but-no-quick-counter-seen" target="_blank" >canceling or delaying sanctions</a> approved by Congress to put pressure on Russia to stem or stop its continued aggression against Ukraine.</p><p>Russia, by providing arms and intelligence to Iran, has enabled it to attack U.S. bases in the Middle East, resulting in the death of American personnel and billions in damage to U.S. assets.</p><p>One can only conclude that these acts of treachery are the actions of Trump working as an agent of Russia. The spineless Republicans have ample justification to impeach Trump on charges of treason. It's time for action. Congress cannot allow these actions to continue without consequences.</p><p><i>Stephen M. Morris, Lincoln Park</i></p><h3>Wealthy elites fear CTU </h3><p>As an elderly Caucasian and lifelong Chicagoan, it always staggers and stuns me the way the wealthy play the working class to serve their ends. Private charter school profiteers haven't been this excited since Rahm Emanuel did their bidding and closed public schools. The destruction of public education has been a long-term goal of the wealthy, resulting in the "CTU Derangement Syndrome" that is the driving force behind all their efforts. It's a standard neoliberal scam: Privatize the profit and socialize the cost.</p><p>Let's face it. A predominantly Black-and-women-run Chicago Teachers Union fills the elite white power class with abject fear. </p><p><i>Edward David Juillard, Morgan Park</i></p>
